title: Why Wall Street is betting big on India’s IPO and financial market boom - The HinduBusinessLine
text:
India’s booming IPO market, expanding financial services sector and growing investor participation are attracting global firms such as Blackstone, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, even as currency weakness and regulatory challenges persist. | Photo Credit: iStockphoto

Across India’s small towns and bustling cities, retail investors have been snapping up shares of newly listed companies. It’s a boom that Blackstone Inc.’s President Jon Gray celebrates thousands of miles away in his Park Avenue office.

“For us, outside of the United States, India is the most liquid market — the easiest place to get an IPO done in the world this year,’’ Gray said in an interview. India already saw one of its biggest ever initial public offerings in recent weeks and a listing with a market value of more than $100 billion is possible from billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s empire, making the country one of the world’s busiest IPO markets.

Gray and other financial heavyweights acknowledge challenges like rising inflation and the falling rupee. Yet, between its private equity and real estate businesses, Blackstone has listed a string of companies over the past decade in India and revenue growth has been high, Gray said. The firm expects assets under management in the South Asian country to double to $100 billion in the coming years.

That’s a sign of the growing sophistication of the financial markets within this $4 trillion economy as it opens up further to foreign money. It’s also a dramatic turnaround from just a few years ago when private equity investors had limited options to exit investments in India, let alone at substantial profits. Now private equity, private credit and sovereign wealth funds are committing ever deeper pools of capital, while market makers like Citadel Securities LLC and hedge funds like Millennium Management LLC have built a presence there. Other parts of the financial industry are also changing swiftly.

India’s markets remain a fraction of China’s by size. High corporate taxes and the rupee’s decline leave foreign firms smaller profits to repatriate into dollars. On the political front, a youth protest movement is creating new pressures for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.

Wall Street bosses are still looking at the economy’s long-term prospects. Many are betting on a series of measures taken by the Modi administration to jumpstart a vast digital payments ecosystem. Millions of Indians are now putting their savings into financial markets for the first time. As new developments reshape Indian finance, here are some of the biggest changes and challenges emerging:

In recent months, a string of Wall Street bosses have landed in India to court businesses and the government. Citigroup Inc.’s Jane Fraser had a meeting with Modi. JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Jamie Dimon met the country’s finance minister. Both firms are working on the IPO of Ambani’s digital services giant Jio Platforms. That company is expected to go public later this year at a valuation that could make it India’s largest ever, Bloomberg News has reported.

Banks have been bolstering teams in investment banking and capital markets. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. has injected at least $500 million into its India banking franchise in recent years, Bloomberg News has reported. It’s also one of the banks on the Jio IPO.

“Rapid financialization of household savings is creating a durable pool of domestic capital to support private-sector investment,” said Sonjoy Chatterjee, chairman and chief executive officer of Goldman Sachs India.

The average fee paid to bankers in India has risen to 1.86% of an IPO’s value, according to capital-markets data provider LSEG. That’s higher than roughly 1.5% in Hong Kong.

The firms are all vying for a larger slice of the pie in what’s become one of the world’s most competitive investment banking markets. The Wall Street banks are competing against each other as well as Japanese ones and local firms like Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. and Axis Bank Ltd., who command deep client relationships and pricing power.

Meanwhile, global banks are seeing other opportunities. Citi's India CEO K. Balasubramanian said in an interview that the bank sees added opportunities to do business with local and foreign corporations as India enters into more trade deals with countries including the UK. The India arm of Japan's Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. plans to expand its rupee-bond business as companies diversify funding, according to a spokesperson. It has managed about 57 billion rupees ($600 million) of local bonds since the inception of its business in September 2025 and aims to significantly enhance its share over the next two to three years. The firm is also expanding in India’s IPO market.

Until the 1990s, India was almost completely closed to foreign capital, and few private equity funds were involved in major deals. As the economy has opened up, PE firms have invested tens of billions of dollars and deal sizes have been increasing.

Brookfield Asset Management Ltd.’s CEO Connor Teskey says that over the next five years the firm’s investment in India will be more than $100 billion from about $30 billion in 2025. It’s a bet on “India’s immense scale, strong economic growth, respect for capital and growing demand for infrastructure,” he said.

Firms like Brookfield and Blackstone are also betting on the country’s real estate markets. Office space has seen a boom as local and foreign companies scramble for room in swanky new towers in cities like Mumbai and New Delhi.

“The one challenge obviously has been higher inflation rates and currency depreciation,” Gray said. Despite that Blackstone has had very good success in areas like its logistics portfolio because “there’s so much underlying demand that you can make up for the fact that the currency’s been going down,” he said.
